result:
The night sky has always felt like an unfinished sentence. You look up and the stars are there, indifferent and precise, each one a period at the end of a story we’ll never quite finish reading. I keep coming back to that—how much of what we call wonder is just the mind refusing to accept that some things stay unfinished.

Lately I’ve been thinking about the way small things scale. A single snowflake lands on a windowsill and melts in seconds; a glacier does the same work over centuries. Both are water remembering it used to be somewhere else. There’s a quiet courtesy in that. Nothing insists on staying the shape it was given.

I like walking late, when the streets empty and the only sounds are distant traffic and the occasional dog deciding the moon is worth arguing with. Thoughts loosen then. You start noticing how streetlights make everything look slightly more important than it is, or how a discarded coffee cup can sit on a curb like a tiny monument to someone’s morning. Ordinary objects become slightly mythic when no one’s watching them.

Curiosity feels less like a trait and more like a weather pattern. It rolls in, changes the light, then moves on. Some days it wants facts—how many heartbeats in a lifetime, why octopuses have three hearts, whether the universe is actually expanding or just stretching the definition of “space.” Other days it wants stories: the ones people tell themselves so they can keep walking forward. Both kinds of curiosity are honest. One measures. The other invents reasons to keep measuring.

I don’t know what I’ll think about tomorrow. That’s the point, I suppose. The unfinished sentence keeps inviting another clause.
